summary.text: 都 combines 邑, marking a settlement, with 者, which cues the sound of the city word. A Western Zhou bronze inscription is reported to use it for a city. Its separate Mandarin reading dōu means “all”; a proposed link to 諸 remains uncertain.

formation.text: This is a phonosemantic compound: 邑 contributes the settlement category, while 者 provides a sound cue for the city reading. The traditional account defines 都 as a settlement containing a former ruler’s ancestral temple, but this does not prove that definition was the word’s earliest meaning or establish the graph’s ultimate pictorial origin.

components.text: 邑 contributes the settlement or city category in 都. The traditional analysis supports this role; no separate earlier form or detailed graphic history is established.
者 is the phonetic component for 都’s city reading. The reconstructed syllables are related but not identical, consistent with a sound cue; they do not establish the graph’s ultimate pictorial origin.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system, 者 is reconstructed as *tjaːʔ and 都 as *taː. Their related initials and finals support a sound comparison, though the forms differ and are reconstructions rather than recorded pronunciations.

history.text: A Western Zhou bronze inscription associated with the 㝬鐘 is reported to contain 都; later bronze examples are also catalogued. This provides an early witness, but the available reports do not establish stroke-by-stroke changes or an original pictorial referent. No oracle-bone form is established in the cited material.
The character’s recorded graphic history supports the settlement-and-sound analysis, but does not show a detailed sequence of changes from an earlier component form.

uncertainties.text: The graph’s original pictorial referent and detailed development remain unresolved; modern shape alone cannot establish them.
The reported senses “elegant,” “great,” “inhabit,” and “gather” lack an established chronology or semantic path in the evidence cited here.
The proposed connection between dōu “all” and 諸 lacks an independently established early pronunciation comparison and borrowing history.

Classical citations record large-city and capital uses. Their chronology relative to the institutional settlement and fief senses is undetermined.

senses.period: Reported in a lexicographic source; exact earliest attestation unresolved
senses.text: The totalizing word is written 都 and read dōu in Mandarin. Its proposed connection to 諸 concerns a possible reuse of the graph for a different word, not a demonstrated change from “city” to “all.” The early sound match remains uncertain.
A classical citation records an elegant or beautiful sense, but its relation to the settlement and city senses is undetermined.
In modern Mandarin, 都 is read dū for city and capital meanings.
In modern Mandarin, 都 is also read dōu for “all” or “the whole.” Its proposed historical connection to 諸 remains uncertain.

limitations.text: The cited senses do not establish transitions among shrine settlement, fief, large city, capital, elegance, and totalizing meaning.
The early history and sound basis of the proposed 諸-to-dōu relationship remain unverified.
The early bronze city use does not prove that “city” was the earliest spoken meaning; the shrine-bearing definition is a later lexicographic account.

evidence.text: city

Phonosemantic compound. ⻏ represents the meaning and 者 represents the sound. Based on the meaning "large city, capital", which is the meaning when pronounced "dū". When pronounced "dōu", it has the unrelated meaning "all", etymologically related to 多 (many).
有先君之舊宗廟曰都。从邑者聲。周禮：距國五百里爲都。
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *taː): phonetic 者 (OC *tjaːʔ) + semantic 邑 (“town, city”).
Colloquial form of 諸 (OC *tja, “all”) (Schuessler, 2007).
有先君之舊宗廟曰都。从邑者聲。周禮：距國五百里爲都。

evidence.source: 《說文解字》, reproduced with 段玉裁’s commentary
evidence.text: The entry defines 都 as an邑 with the former ruler’s ancestral temple and says it is formed from 邑 with 者 as phonetic. Duan’s commentary quotes the Zuozhuan definition and discusses the Zhou ritual and fief senses. This supports the traditional component analysis, but it is a Han lexicographic account, not direct proof of the character’s earliest formation.
evidence.title: 都 dū、dōu - 汉典

evidence.source: 《左傳·莊公二十八年》, quoted in Han Dian
evidence.text: The quoted definition distinguishes an邑 containing the ancestral shrine and ancestral spirit tablet, called a 都, from one without them. This is evidence for a specifically institutional settlement sense, not evidence that “capital” was the earliest spoken meaning.
evidence.title: 都 dū、dōu - 汉典

evidence.source: 《周禮》 and 《左傳》 citations listed in Han Dian
evidence.text: The entry cites 《周禮》 for a 都 as a territorial/fief category and 《左傳·隱公元年》 for a large 都. It also cites 《史記》 for 都 as a capital and another 《史記》 passage for a city. These references suggest that the institutional settlement/fief and larger urban/capital uses were distinct attested senses; the entry does not date the underlying spoken extensions precisely.
evidence.title: 都 dū、dōu - 汉典

evidence.text: The dictionary gives 都, 凡也 (“都 means all/entire”) for totalizing uses, and records senses such as “beautiful,” “great,” “inhabit,” and “gather.” This is a lexicographic report of attested glosses, not proof that these senses developed chronologically from the settlement meaning.
evidence.title: 都 dū、dōu - 汉典

evidence.source: 《廣雅》 bibliographic description; CText access attempt failed
evidence.text: Search results identify 《廣雅》 as a lexicon compiled by Zhang Yi around 227 CE, but the primary text page returned a 403 during inspection. I therefore could not independently inspect the cited 都，凡也 entry in that edition.
evidence.title: 廣雅 - 中國哲學書電子化計劃

evidence.source: Wiktionary, drawing on Zhengzhang’s phonetic-series data and Baxter–Sagart reconstruction
evidence.text: The listed phonetic-series analysis gives 都 *taː in Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system and *tˤa in Baxter–Sagart’s system; 者 is listed as *tjaːʔ and *tjaːʔ, respectively. These are reconstructions in different systems, not direct recordings. The modern Mandarin reading of the city sense is dū; the entry also gives Middle Chinese tu. The sound comparison supports a phonetic role for 者 in the compound, while the reconstructed difference between the two elements shows that “phonetic” need not mean identical reconstructed syllables.
evidence.title: 都 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: The authors’ supplementary site identifies their 2014 book Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction and provides Old Chinese reconstruction lists. The site supports identifying *tˤa as a Baxter–Sagart-system reconstruction, not as an attested pronunciation.
evidence.title: The Baxter-Sagart reconstruction of Old Chinese

evidence.source: Han Dian; compared with Wiktionary’s phonetic-series listing
evidence.text: Han Dian records a totalizing 都 sense and quotes the gloss 都，凡也; Wiktionary separately reports the proposal that the all-reading is a colloquial form of 諸, citing Schuessler (2007). The record does not establish that the semantic “all” sense developed from city/meeting-place imagery. The proposed 諸 connection concerns a word/read­ing written with 都, and must be kept distinct from 者 functioning as a sound component inside the city graph. I found no inspected primary historical source here that establishes the proposed colloquial pronunciation or independently documents the sound match at its earliest stage.
evidence.title: 都 dū、dōu - 汉典

evidence.text: The entry reports Standard Mandarin Pinyin dū for the capital-city reading and dōu for the totalizing reading, Cantonese Guangzhou/Hong Kong Jyutping dou1 for its listed reading, and historical comparisons for the city reading: Middle Chinese tu, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *tˤa, and Zhengzhang Old Chinese *taː. Its cited phonetic-series table gives 者 *tjaːʔ in Zhengzhang’s system. These data concern the graphic 都 and proposed phonetic 者; they do not independently demonstrate the history of the separate dōu “all” word.
evidence.title: 都 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: The entry’s glyph-history section lists bronze examples as 㝬鐘 (Western Zhou late), 𦅫鎛 (Spring and Autumn middle), 洹子孟姜壺 (Spring and Autumn late), and 中都戈 (Spring and Autumn). It also lists Chu manuscripts, Shuowen small seal, Qin slips, Han slips and transmitted ancient forms. I did not visually inspect the glyph images, so these listings support reported artifact/date associations only; they do not support detailed claims about stroke-by-stroke graphic change, corruption, or a specific original pictorial referent. The listed witnesses provide a Zhou-to-Qin/Han trail, but not an oracle-bone form.
evidence.title: 都 dū、dōu - 汉典

evidence.field: component function and current graphic structure
evidence.text: The dictionary labels the form phonosemantic, from 邑 with 者 as sound; the page reports the modern left-right structure and gives a glyph-history list. This supports the traditional semantic component account: 邑/阝 signals settlement or city. No inspected source established an earlier ancestor, corruption, or a precise historical transformation from a distinct component shape; no chronology should be inferred from those shapes alone.
evidence.title: 都 dū、dōu - 汉典

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The database analyzes bronze-inscription 都 as 者 plus 邑, with 者 serving as the phonetic element, and reports the meaning as a city or capital. It cites the 㝬鐘 inscription 扑伐厥都. This supports an early city use and the component analysis; it does not establish the graph’s ultimate pictorial origin.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: Shuowen analysis and dated sense citations
evidence.text: The entry reproduces 說文’s account: 都 is an 邑 containing a former ruler’s ancestral temple, formed from 邑 with 者 as phonetic. It separately cites 《左傳·莊公二十八年》 for the distinction between shrine-bearing 都 and other 邑; 《史記》 for large-city and capital uses; 《詩經·鄭風·有女同車》 for 都 meaning elegant or beautiful; and later texts for totalizing and verbal uses. These references attest reported senses but do not alone prove a chronology or semantic path among them.
evidence.title: [A04214] 都 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Wiktionary, reporting Zhengzhang Shangfang and Middle Chinese readings
evidence.text: The page gives Standard Mandarin dū for the city reading, Middle Chinese tu, Zhengzhang Old Chinese *taː for 都 and *tjaːʔ for 者, and lists 都 in the 者 phonetic series. These are system-specific reconstructions rather than recorded ancient pronunciations. Their related initials and finals are consistent with a phonetic role despite differences in reconstructed syllable details.
evidence.title: 都 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: For the city reading, the page reports Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *tˤa for 都 and gives the 2014 reconstruction-system label. This differs in notation and detail from Zhengzhang’s *taː. It is reconstructed evidence for the graph’s reading, not an attestation.
evidence.title: 都 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: The page reports a proposal that the totalizing word written 都 is a colloquial form of 諸. This is a proposal about a word represented by the whole graph, distinct from the role of 者 as a sound component inside the city graph. The sources inspected here do not independently establish the early pronunciation and borrowing relationship, so this remains unverified.
evidence.title: 都 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

search_audit.query: 都 金文 字形 演变 说文 邑 者声
search_audit.outcome: Searched and inspected the Ministry of Education character entry, CUHK database, and Han Dian entry. The inspected sources support a bronze-inscription city use and traditional component analysis, while not establishing the graph’s pictorial origin or a detailed sequence of graphic change.

search_audit.query: 都 bronze inscription form paleography 者 邑 character
search_audit.outcome: Inspected the Commons bronze and seal file descriptions. The bronze file gives a specific 㝬鐘 source association and CC0 reuse terms; both are modern vector redrawings. The seal candidate is a Shuowen-style drawing, not an artifact image.

search_audit.query: site:en.wiktionary.org/wiki/都 都 Old Chinese 者 phonetic series
search_audit.outcome: Inspected entries for 都, 者, and 諸. The entries report modern and reconstructed readings and the 者 phonetic-series relationship; the reported proposal linking dōu ‘all’ to 諸 was not independently established from primary historical evidence.

search_audit.query: 都 小學堂 字形演變 金文
search_audit.outcome: Opened the supplied query-form URL and official license page. The query page loaded without character-specific image results in the inspected content, and the license page returned no readable text, so no Xiaoxuetang candidate was selected.

gaps: No oracle-bone form was established in the inspected sources; earliest listed graphic witnesses here are bronze inscriptions attributed to Western Zhou and later periods.
Glyph images were not visually inspected; stroke-level graphic evolution, possible corruption, and original pictorial referent remain undetermined.
The Shuowen definition is a Han-era lexicographic account, not independent proof that shrine-bearing settlement was the earliest spoken sense.

The sources report the dōu totalizing sense and a proposed relationship to colloquial 諸, but an early attestation and independently supported historical sound match for that word relationship were not established.
No inspected evidence dates the transitions from shrine settlement to fief, large city, and national capital, nor establishes the semantic links among “beautiful,” “great,” “gather,” and “all.”

A second primary Old Chinese reconstruction list entry for 者 was not directly checked; the same-page phonetic-series data give a Zhengzhang reconstruction, while the Baxter–Sagart comparison is reported through Wiktionary.
The Shuowen and CText source pages had access limitations or provided only search-result excerpts; these failures are recorded above.

No inspected source established an oracle-bone form for 都. The bronze example identified by the Commons file is attributed to the Western Zhou 㝬鐘; the modern vector image is not an artifact photograph.
The graphic evidence supports the reported components and an early city use, but does not settle the original pictorial referent, possible corruption, or step-by-step graphic changes.

The 說文 shrine-bearing settlement definition is a Han-era lexicographic account; it cannot by itself prove the earliest spoken sense. The sources cite city, capital, elegant, and totalizing senses but do not establish the semantic links or dates of transitions between them.
The dōu ‘all’ relationship to 諸 remains a reported proposal. This research did not independently verify early attestations and a historical sound match for the proposed whole-word borrowing.
The Academia Sinica query URL exposed no character-specific result in the inspected page, and the rights page provided no readable text in this access. No image from that interface was used.
The direct Commons original-image link returned an unsupported SVG content-type error when opened through the web tool; the file description page itself was inspected for identity and rights.

items.period: Western Zhou (approximate attribution of the source form)
items.tradition: Bronze inscription form; modern vector redraw
items.caption: This Western Zhou bronze-script form of 都 is associated with the 㝬鐘 inscription. It was used for a city and is analyzed as combining 邑, the settlement element, with 者 as a phonetic element.
items.alt: Black brushlike bronze-script glyph on a white background, with a tall branching form at left, a loop at upper right, and additional angular strokes below.
items.selection_reason: This candidate gives a useful early example of the character and its reported component analysis. The image shows the overall form, while the cited sources support its inscription association, city use, and components.
items.rights: CC0 1.0; modern vector representation released under CC0 according to the Commons file page.

limitations.text: The image is a modern vector redraw, not a photograph or rubbing of the bronze. The source associates it with the 㝬鐘, but the original pictorial referent and step-by-step graphic development remain uncertain.
